l: Ask in Any Modality, Ask in Any Modality, Introduction & Background
s: This unit explains how large language models have advanced while remaining vulnerable to hallucinations, outdated knowledge, and unverifiable reasoning. It describes Retrieval-Augmented Generation as a retriever-generator pipeline that grounds responses in external knowledge, and presents multimodal learning as a way to integrate text, images, audio, and video. It defines multimodal RAG as extending retrieval and generation across heterogeneous modalities, with challenges involving modality selection, fusion, and cross-modal relevance. The unit also introduces a mathematical formulation for multimodal RAG and outlines datasets, benchmarks, evaluation methods, applications, and the survey’s taxonomy and contributions.

l: Large Language Models, Ask in Any Modality, Introduction & Background
s: Large language models have progressed through advances in transformer architectures, computational resources, and large-scale datasets. They perform well on instruction following, reasoning, in-context learning, and multilingual translation, but face hallucinations, outdated knowledge, and a lack of verifiable reasoning because their parametric memory limits access to up-to-date information.

l: MLLMs, Ask in Any Modality, Introduction & Background
s: Multimodal large language models broaden language-model capabilities by enabling reasoning and generation across multiple data modalities. GPT-4 is identified as demonstrating human-level performance by jointly processing text and images.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Ask in Any Modality, Introduction & Background
s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation addresses limitations of language models by retrieving and incorporating external knowledge, improving factual accuracy and reducing hallucinations. Its retriever-generator pipeline uses embedding models and possible re-ranking to select relevant passages, which the generator then uses to produce more informed and coherent responses. Planning-guided retrieval, agentic RAG, and feedback-driven iterative refinement have further advanced its retrieval and generation components.

l: multimodal learning, Ask in Any Modality, Introduction & Background
s: Multimodal learning enables systems to integrate and reason over heterogeneous data sources for more comprehensive representations. CLIP aligned visual and textual modalities through contrastive learning, inspiring subsequent models and supporting applications including sentiment analysis and biomedical tasks. The field facilitates joint processing of text, images, audio, and video and is presented as a critical enabler of progress toward artificial general intelligence.

l: multimodal RAG, Ask in Any Modality, Introduction & Background
s: Multimodal RAG incorporates sources such as images, audio, and structured data to enrich contextual grounding and improve generation quality. It leverages cross-modal cues for reasoning but introduces challenges involving modality selection, effective fusion, and cross-modal relevance. In the presented formulation, modality-specific encoders map documents into a shared semantic space, a retrieval model selects documents using relevance thresholds, and a generative model produces a response from the query and retrieved context.

l: datasets, Ask in Any Modality, Introduction & Background
s: Datasets support multimodal RAG tasks such as multimodal summarization, visual question answering, and video understanding. The unit states that the survey reviews diverse datasets and provides open-access dataset resources to facilitate future research.

l: benchmarks, Ask in Any Modality, Introduction & Background
s: Benchmarks are used to evaluate multimodal RAG systems across tasks including multimodal summarization, visual question answering, and video understanding. The survey reviews benchmarks and describes evaluation methods covering retrieval performance, generation quality, and modality alignment.

l: Ask in Any Modality, Ask in Any Modality, Key Innovations and Methodologies / 3.1
s: This unit concerns retrieval strategies for multimodal RAG systems, including efficient similarity search, modality-specific retrieval, document retrieval, and re-ranking. It describes multimodal encoders such as CLIP, BLIP, MARVEL, and Uni-IR, as well as maximum inner product search, adaptive quantization, hybrid sparse–dense retrieval, and distributed approximate nearest-neighbor methods. It surveys text-, vision-, video-, audio-, and document-centric retrieval techniques, including systems that use layout, temporal, acoustic, or lexical information. It also explains how re-ranking, relevance scoring, filtering, and optimized example selection improve the quality and robustness of retrieved evidence.

l: multimodal RAG, Ask in Any Modality, Key Innovations and Methodologies / 3.1
s: Multimodal RAG systems encode diverse input modalities into unified embedding spaces to support cross-modal retrieval. The unit describes their use of modality-specific retrieval, efficient similarity search, document understanding, re-ranking, relevance scoring, and filtering.

l: retrieval strategies, Ask in Any Modality, Key Innovations and Methodologies / 3.1
s: Retrieval strategies in multimodal RAG include efficient similarity retrieval, modality-centric retrieval, document retrieval, and re-ranking and selection. They address retrieval precision, computational cost, modality-specific characteristics, temporal and layout information, and evidence quality.

l: efficient search and similarity retrieval, Ask in Any Modality, Key Innovations and Methodologies / 3.1
s: Efficient search and similarity retrieval methods aim to retrieve relevant multimodal evidence from large embedding collections with low latency. The unit discusses MIPS, adaptive quantization, hybrid sparse–dense retrieval, distributed search, ScaNN, MAXSIM, approximate KNN, and learned index structures.

l: multimodal encoders, Ask in Any Modality, Key Innovations and Methodologies / 3.1
s: Multimodal encoders map visual, textual, and other modality representations into spaces that support cross-modal retrieval. CLIP-based methods are described as computationally challenging, while BLIP-inspired approaches use cross-modal attention and later systems such as MARVEL and Uni-IR improve inter-modal discrimination through contrastive training, hard-negative mining, and balanced sampling.

l: ColPali, Ask in Any Modality, Key Innovations and Methodologies / 3.1
s: ColPali performs end-to-end document image retrieval by embedding page patches with a vision-language backbone and bypassing OCR. It is also described as using consensus-based filtering and multi-vector mapping to remove low-similarity candidates.

l: maximum inner product search, Ask in Any Modality, Key Innovations and Methodologies / 3.1
s: Maximum inner product search provides sublinear lookup by approximating top-k inner products for large embedding collections. Multimodal RAG systems such as MuRAG and RA-CM3 use approximate MIPS, although coarse quantization can reduce recall.

l: adaptive quantization, Ask in Any Modality, Key Innovations and Methodologies / 3.1
s: Adaptive quantization dynamically allocates bits to dense regions of an embedding distribution. The unit states that it improves recall compared with static quantization schemes and is used to mitigate the recall degradation caused by coarse quantization.

l: hybrid sparse–dense retrieval, Ask in Any Modality, Key Innovations and Methodologies / 3.1
s: Hybrid sparse–dense retrieval combines dense embeddings with sparse lexical signals. It complements semantic similarity with lexical evidence in multimodal retrieval systems.

l: modality-centric retrieval, Ask in Any Modality, Key Innovations and Methodologies / 3.1
s: Modality-centric retrieval exploits the distinct characteristics of text, images, video, audio, and documents. The unit organizes this approach into text-centric, vision-centric, video-centric, audio-centric, and document retrieval.

l: text-centric retrieval, Ask in Any Modality, Key Innovations and Methodologies / 3.1
s: Text-centric retrieval uses traditional lexical methods such as BM25 and dense retrievers such as MiniLM and BGE-M3 for text-based evidence retrieval. ColBERT and PreFLMR preserve fine-grained token interactions, while RAFT and CRAG improve accurate citation of text spans.

l: BM25, Ask in Any Modality, Key Innovations and Methodologies / 3.1
s: BM25 is presented as a foundational traditional method for text-centric retrieval. It is also incorporated into ranking and relevance-scoring frameworks such as RAGTrans and OMG-QA.

l: vision-centric retrieval, Ask in Any Modality, Key Innovations and Methodologies / 3.1
s: Vision-centric retrieval uses image representations to extract knowledge and retrieve visually similar content. Systems such as EchoSight and ImgRet use reference images as queries, while composed image retrieval methods combine multiple image features for zero-shot retrieval.

l: video-centric retrieval, Ask in Any Modality, Key Innovations and Methodologies / 3.1
s: Video-centric retrieval extends visual retrieval with temporal dynamics and video-language modeling. The unit describes incremental retrieval, auxiliary OCR and ASR text, dual-channel and graph-based grounding, contrastive transformer hashing, reversed-video hard negatives, and divide-and-conquer processing for long or complex videos.

l: audio-centric retrieval, Ask in Any Modality, Key Innovations and Methodologies / 3.1
s: Audio-centric retrieval seeks to improve contextual alignment and real-time processing while reducing reliance on traditional ASR pipelines. WavRAG and SEAL map raw audio into shared latent spaces, while other systems use retrieved acoustic or textual context for synthesis, captioning, ASR correction, and handling noisy audio.

l: document retrieval, Ask in Any Modality, Key Innovations and Methodologies / 3.1
s: Document retrieval increasingly integrates textual, visual, and layout information across entire documents. ColPali, ColQwen2, and M3DocVQA support page- or multi-page retrieval and reasoning, while ViTLP, DocLLM, CREAM, mPLUG-DocOwl, and SV-RAG address layout understanding, efficiency, format unification, or evidence-page retrieval.

l: re-ranking and selection strategies, Ask in Any Modality, Key Innovations and Methodologies / 3.1
s: Re-ranking and selection strategies prioritize retrieved candidates through optimized example selection, relevance scoring, and filtering. They use multi-step retrieval, probabilistic or statistical calibration, clustering for diverse video key frames, multimodal similarity measures, hierarchical confidence scores, hard-negative mining, consensus filtering, and dynamic modality filtering.

l: Ask in Any Modality, Ask in Any Modality, 3.2
s: The unit categorizes multimodal fusion methods into Score Fusion and Alignment Models, Attention-Based Mechanisms, and Unified Frameworks and Projections. Score Fusion and Alignment Models use shared embedding spaces, score fusion, feature fusion, and projection strategies to align modalities, with MegaPairs combining CLIP-based and MLLM-based retrieval at the cost of increased inference complexity. Attention-Based Mechanisms dynamically regulate cross-modal interactions through cross-attention, co-attention, memory retrieval, and related strategies, although some require task-specific supervision or substantial computation. Unified Frameworks and Projections consolidate multimodal inputs through unified tensors, joint-grained retrieval, captioning, shared decoders, and dense-to-sparse projection.

l: Fusion Mechanisms, Ask in Any Modality, 3.2
s: Fusion Mechanisms in this unit are organized into score fusion and alignment, attention-based, and unified framework or projection approaches for integrating multimodal representations.

l: Score Fusion and Alignment Models, Ask in Any Modality, 3.2
s: Score Fusion and Alignment Models align multimodal representations through textual conversion, shared embedding spaces, score or feature fusion, attention-score injection, joint queries, prototype-based mappings, and projection methods. The approaches described balance semantic alignment and retrieval quality against costs such as inference complexity, retrieval noise, reduced modality specificity, or limited interpretability.

l: Attention-Based Mechanisms, Ask in Any Modality, 3.2
s: Attention-Based Mechanisms dynamically modulate interactions between modalities using cross-attention, co-attention, memory retrieval, gated attention, and mutual-guided alignment. They support fine-grained multimodal reasoning but can require task-specific attention heads, aligned supervision, or substantial computation.

l: Unified Frameworks and Projections, Ask in Any Modality, 3.2
s: Unified Frameworks and Projections consolidate multimodal inputs into coherent representations through hierarchical fusion, iterative integration, flattened embedding tensors, joint-grained retrieval, caption-based conversion, shared decoders, and dense-to-sparse projection. These methods aim to improve consistency, richness, storage efficiency, or interpretability.

l: MegaPairs, Ask in Any Modality, 3.2
s: MegaPairs embeds images and queries into a shared CLIP space and scales this approach by integrating both CLIP-based and MLLM-based retrieval. It fuses their scores to exploit complementary strengths, but this increases inference complexity.

l: CLIP, Ask in Any Modality, 3.2
s: CLIP is used to embed images and queries into a shared space in Wiki-LLaVA, C3Net, Riedler and Langer, and MegaPairs. It also contributes to score fusion in the interleaved image-text approach of Sharifymoghaddam et al. (2024), while MegaPairs combines CLIP-based retrieval with MLLM-based retrieval.

l: BLIP, Ask in Any Modality, 3.2
s: BLIP contributes to feature fusion in the interleaved image-text approach of Sharifymoghaddam et al. (2024). A BLIP-inspired Query Transformer is also used by MA-LMM to align video-text embeddings.

l: M3DocRAG, Ask in Any Modality, 3.2
s: M3DocRAG flattens multi-page documents into a single embedding tensor as part of a unified multimodal representation strategy.

l: Ask in Any Modality, Ask in Any Modality, 3.3
s: Augmentation techniques refine retrieved data before generation to improve multimodal interpretation, structuring, and integration. Context Enrichment expands or refines retrieved knowledge with additional contextual elements, as shown by EMERGE, MiRAG, Video-RAG, and Img2Loc. Adaptive and Iterative Retrieval dynamically adjusts retrieval based on query complexity, modality, granularity, relevance, and prior feedback. Systems including UniversalRAG, SKURG, OmniSearch, OMGM, IRAMIG, OMG-QA, and RAGAR use these strategies to improve retrieval precision and contextual consistency.

l: augmentation, Ask in Any Modality, 3.3
s: Augmentation techniques refine retrieved data before it is passed to generation, improving multimodal interpretation, structuring, and integration.

l: retrieved data, Ask in Any Modality, 3.3
s: Retrieved data is refined or expanded before generation through additional text chunks, image tokens, structured data, entity relationships, semantic descriptions, and auxiliary multimodal context.

l: Context Enrichment, Ask in Any Modality, 3.3
s: Context Enrichment enhances the relevance of retrieved knowledge by refining or expanding it with additional contextual elements. EMERGE, MiRAG, Video-RAG, and Img2Loc use entity information, query reformulation, structured retrieval requests, or similar and dissimilar points to improve grounding and reasoning.

l: Adaptive and Iterative Retrieval, Ask in Any Modality, 3.3
s: Adaptive and Iterative Retrieval dynamically adjusts retrieval according to query complexity, required modality, granularity, relevance, and feedback from earlier steps. It includes methods that route queries, determine retrieval hops, filter irrelevant content, decompose multimodal queries, update queries, and progressively refine results.

l: multimodal retrieval, Ask in Any Modality, 3.3
s: Multimodal retrieval is improved by dynamically updating queries based on retrieved content, as in IRAMIG, and by using multimodal reranking and fine-grained textual filtering, as in OMGM. RAGAR also adjusts retrieval through prior responses and multimodal analysis to enhance contextual consistency.

l: Ask in Any Modality, Ask in Any Modality, 3.4
s: This unit reviews generation techniques for multimodal RAG, including in-context learning, reasoning, instruction tuning, source attribution, and agentic interaction. In-context learning methods use retrieved multimodal content or examples to improve reasoning without retraining, while reasoning methods apply chain-of-thought, evidence curation, verification, and compositional strategies. Instruction-tuning approaches train or preference-tune models to improve visual understanding, retrieval decisions, ranking, and resistance to overreliance on retrieved context. The unit also discusses evidence citation and attribution limitations, as well as agent-driven systems for user interaction, specialized applications, and hierarchical multimodal reasoning.

l: Generation Techniques, Ask in Any Modality, 3.4
s: Generation Techniques in multimodal RAG include in-context learning, reasoning, instruction tuning, source attribution and evidence transparency, and agentic generation and interaction. These techniques improve response quality, reasoning, evidence use, and interaction across multimodal applications.

l: In-Context Learning, Ask in Any Modality, 3.4
s: In-Context Learning uses retrieved content as few-shot examples to enhance reasoning in multimodal RAG without retraining. RMR, Sharifymoghaddam et al. (2024), RA-CM3, RAG-Driver, MSIER, and Raven extend or refine this approach through retrieved experiences, multimodal example scoring, and Fusion-in-Context Learning.

l: retrieval augmentation, Ask in Any Modality, 3.4
s: Retrieval augmentation enhances multimodal RAG reasoning by supplying retrieved content as examples. It is used in approaches such as RMR, RA-CM3, and RAG-Driver, although retrieval can miss evidence distributed across sections or documents.

l: multimodal RAG, Ask in Any Modality, 3.4
s: Multimodal RAG is improved through in-context learning, chain-of-thought reasoning, instruction tuning, evidence attribution, and agentic systems. The discussed methods address reasoning, retrieval, ranking, evidence integration, hallucination reduction, and interaction across visual and textual information.

l: Reasoning, Ask in Any Modality, 3.4
s: Reasoning methods decompose complex tasks into sequential or branching steps to improve coherence and robustness in multimodal RAG. RAGAR, VisDoM, SAM-RAG, and LDRE use branching paths, evidence curation, multi-stage verification, or refined descriptions for fact-checking and composed image retrieval.

l: chain of thought, Ask in Any Modality, 3.4
s: Chain of thought decomposes complex reasoning into sequential steps. RAGAR extends reasoning with Chain of RAG and Tree of RAG, while VisDoM and SAM-RAG combine chain-of-thought with evidence curation and multi-stage verification.

l: Instruction Tuning, Ask in Any Modality, 3.4
s: Instruction Tuning is used to fine-tune or instruct-tune generation components for specific applications. The cited approaches improve visual feature extraction, prompt generation, adaptive retrieval, evidence identification, ranking, image-difference description, knowledge balancing, and generation quality.

l: MLLMs, Ask in Any Modality, 3.4
s: MLLMs are used to score textual and visual relevance in MSIER and to invoke retrieval adaptively, identify relevant evidence, and improve ranking in MR2AG and RagVL. Other methods train or refine MLLMs through instruction tuning, preference fine-tuning, or direct preference optimization.

l: Source Attribution and Evidence Transparency, Ask in Any Modality, 3.4
s: Source Attribution and Evidence Transparency is a significant focus in multimodal RAG. OMG-QA prompts for explicit evidence citation, MuRAR integrates multimodal information from source-based retrieval, and VISA highlights visual evidence in retrieved screenshots, though attribution and recall degrade when evidence is distributed or requires cross-modal integration.

l: source attribution, Ask in Any Modality, 3.4
s: Source attribution is supported by explicit evidence citations in OMG-QA and visual evidence highlighting in VISA. Its accuracy can decline when evidence spans multiple sections or requires cross-modal integration, and MuRAR's recall can be limited when relevant evidence is scattered across documents.

l: Agentic Generation and Interaction, Ask in Any Modality, 3.4
s: Agentic Generation and Interaction uses autonomous or semi-autonomous systems for user interaction, specialized applications, and complex reasoning over multimodal data. AppAgent v2, USER-LLM R1, MMAD, Yi et al. (2025), CollEX, HM-RAG, and CogPlanner support GUI navigation, personalization, anomaly detection, clinical reporting, collection exploration, multi-agent collaboration, and adaptive planning.

l: agent-driven multimodal RAG, Ask in Any Modality, 3.4
s: Agent-driven multimodal RAG applies autonomous or semi-autonomous systems across diverse interaction paradigms and specialized domains, often producing complex outputs. HM-RAG coordinates hierarchical multi-agent collaboration across multimodal data streams, while CogPlanner iteratively refines queries and adaptively selects retrieval strategies.

l: Ask in Any Modality, Ask in Any Modality, 3.5
s: Training Strategies for multimodal RAG models use multiple stages to capture cross-modal interactions. Pretraining on paired datasets establishes cross-modal relationships, while fine-tuning adapts models to task-specific objectives. REVEAL combines Prefix Language Modeling Loss with contrastive, disentangled regularization, and alignment regularization losses before using cross-entropy for downstream tasks. Contrastive learning methods, including InfoNCE loss and several refinements, improve multimodal retrieval and generation by aligning positives and separating negatives.

l: Training Strategies, Ask in Any Modality, 3.5
s: Training Strategies for multimodal RAG models involve pretraining followed by fine-tuning. They include objectives such as language modeling, contrastive learning, regularization, alignment, and cross-entropy losses.

l: multimodal RAG models, Ask in Any Modality, 3.5
s: Multimodal RAG models are trained through multiple stages to capture cross-modal interactions. They use contrastive and other specialized losses to improve retrieval-augmented generation.

l: pretraining, Ask in Any Modality, 3.5
s: Pretraining on large paired datasets establishes cross-modal relationships. In REVEAL, pretraining optimizes Prefix Language Modeling Loss, with additional contrastive and regularization losses.

l: fine-tuning, Ask in Any Modality, 3.5
s: Fine-tuning adapts models to task-specific objectives by aligning outputs with task requirements. It employs a cross-entropy objective for downstream tasks such as visual question answering or image captioning.

l: REVEAL, Ask in Any Modality, 3.5
s: REVEAL integrates multiple training objectives. Its pretraining uses Prefix Language Modeling Loss, Contrastive Loss, Disentangled Regularization Loss, and Alignment Regularization Loss, while fine-tuning uses cross-entropy for downstream tasks.

l: contrastive learning, Ask in Any Modality, 3.5
s: Contrastive learning improves representation quality by pulling positive pairs closer and pushing negative pairs apart in the embedding space. Refinements include visually similar but semantically distinct negatives, adversarial captions, hard negative documents, expert-annotated data, auxiliary MSE loss, and synthetic positive pairs.

l: InfoNCE loss, Ask in Any Modality, 3.5
s: InfoNCE loss is widely employed in multimodal RAG models, including VISRAG, MegaPairs, and SAM-RAG. It improves retrieval-augmented generation by supporting contrastive alignment.

l: Ask in Any Modality, Ask in Any Modality, Open Problems and Future Directions
s: The unit identifies open challenges for multimodal RAG systems in generalization, explainability, robustness, reasoning, alignment, retrieval, and agent-based operation. It reports that multimodal RAG systems can exhibit domain-adaptation difficulties, modality biases, weak attribution, vulnerability to adversarial perturbations, and degradation from low-quality or outdated sources. It highlights compositional reasoning, modality alignment, knowledge graphs, unified embedding spaces, and feedback-driven retrieval as important research directions. It also connects agent-based multimodal RAGs, real-world sensory data, and embodied AI with future applications in robotics, navigation, physics-informed reasoning, and AGI.

l: multimodal RAG, Ask in Any Modality, Open Problems and Future Directions
s: Multimodal RAG systems often struggle with domain adaptation, modality biases, compositional reasoning, explainability, and robustness. They may over-rely on text, produce different-quality answers depending on the modalities used, and degrade when sources are low-quality or outdated.

l: explainability, Ask in Any Modality, Open Problems and Future Directions
s: Explainability remains a major challenge because multimodal RAG systems often attribute responses to broad sources, such as entire documents or large visual regions, rather than identifying exact contributing elements across modalities.

l: robustness, Ask in Any Modality, Open Problems and Future Directions
s: Robustness remains an open challenge and a crucial research direction for multimodal RAGs. These systems are vulnerable to adversarial perturbations, misleading images, low-quality or outdated sources, and knowledge poisoning.

l: cross-modal retrieval, Ask in Any Modality, Open Problems and Future Directions
s: Cross-modal retrieval can be hijacked by a few adversarial knowledge injections, as demonstrated by MM-PoisonRAG and Poisoned-MRAG, causing generation to derail.

l: knowledge poisoning, Ask in Any Modality, Open Problems and Future Directions
s: Knowledge poisoning can allow adversarial knowledge injections to hijack cross-modal retrieval and derail generation in multimodal RAG systems. Robust defense mechanisms against it are described as imperative.
